learn: Governments keep order, provide security and public services, and protect rights.
Forms include democracy, monarchy, oligarchy and authoritarian rule.
Direct democracy: citizens vote on laws. Representative democracy: citizens elect lawmakers.
check: A purpose of government is to...
lessons.try: Compare how three forms of government make decisions.

learn: John Locke argued people have natural rights to life, liberty and property.
Montesquieu proposed separation of powers.
Rousseau described a social contract between people and government.
check: Locke named rights to life, liberty and...
The social contract was described by...
lessons.try: Match each thinker's idea to a part of the Constitution.

learn: Magna Carta (1215) limited the king's power.
The English Bill of Rights (1689) protected Parliament and some individual rights.
Colonial assemblies and town meetings practised self-government.
lessons.try: Trace an idea from Magna Carta to the Bill of Rights.

learn: The Declaration of Independence (1776) explained why the colonies broke from Britain.
It stated that governments get their power from the consent of the governed.
The Treaty of Paris (1783) ended the war.
check: The Declaration was written mainly by...
lessons.try: Summarise the Declaration's theory of government in your own words.

learn: The Articles (1781) created a weak central government with no executive and no power to tax.
Shays' Rebellion (1786-87) showed the government's weakness.
Amending the Articles required every state to agree.
check: Under the Articles, Congress could not...
Shays' Rebellion showed the government was...
lessons.try: List the weaknesses of the Articles.

learn: In 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia and wrote a new Constitution.
The Great Compromise created a House (by population) and a Senate (equal).
The Three-Fifths Compromise counted enslaved people unjustly for representation.
lessons.try: Role-play a debate between large and small states.

learn: Popular sovereignty: the people hold power.
Limited government: the government has only the powers given to it.
The rule of law applies to everyone, including leaders.
check: Popular sovereignty means power belongs to the...
The rule of law applies to...
lessons.try: Find examples of these principles in the Preamble.

lessons.t: Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances
learn: Legislative makes laws, executive enforces them, judicial interprets them.
Each branch can check the others: veto, override, judicial review, appointments.
This prevents any branch from becoming too powerful.
check: Congress overrides a veto with a ___ vote.
lessons.try: Diagram checks and balances among the branches.

learn: Federalists supported the Constitution; Anti-Federalists demanded a bill of rights.
The Federalist Papers (Hamilton, Madison, Jay) argued for ratification.
Amendments need two-thirds of Congress and three-fourths of states; there are 27.
check: Amendments need ___ of states to ratify.
lessons.try: Compare a Federalist and an Anti-Federalist argument.

learn: Congress has a House of Representatives (435 members, 2-year terms) and a Senate (100 members, 6-year terms).
House seats are reapportioned after each census.
The Speaker leads the House; the vice president presides over the Senate.
check: The House is led by the...
lessons.try: Find your representatives and senators.

learn: Enumerated powers: tax, borrow, regulate commerce, declare war, coin money.
The Necessary and Proper Clause gives implied powers.
The Senate confirms appointments and ratifies treaties.
check: Declaring war is a power of...
Implied powers come from the ___ Clause.
lessons.try: Classify powers as enumerated or implied.

learn: A bill is introduced, sent to committee, debated and voted on in both chambers.
Differences are resolved in a conference committee.
The president signs or vetoes; Congress can override.
check: A filibuster can delay a vote in the...
lessons.try: Track a real bill through Congress.

learn: The president must be 35, a natural-born citizen and a US resident for 14 years.
Terms are four years; the 22nd Amendment limits presidents to two elected terms.
The line of succession begins with the vice president and Speaker.
check: The minimum age for president is...
The 22nd Amendment limits presidents to two...
After the vice president, succession goes to the...
lessons.try: Research how the 25th Amendment handles presidential disability.

learn: Roles: chief executive, commander in chief, chief diplomat, chief legislator, head of state.
Executive orders direct federal agencies.
The president nominates judges and appoints officials with Senate approval.
check: As commander in chief, the president leads the...
lessons.try: Find an example of each presidential role in the news.

learn: Fifteen executive departments are led by the cabinet.
Independent agencies (EPA, NASA) and regulatory commissions carry out laws.
Civil servants are hired by merit.
lessons.try: Choose an agency and explain how it affects daily life.

learn: The Supreme Court has nine justices serving during good behaviour (effectively for life).
District courts hold trials; courts of appeals review decisions.
Judges are appointed to protect independence.
lessons.try: Diagram the federal court system.

learn: Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review.
The Court can strike down laws that violate the Constitution.
Judicial philosophies include restraint and activism.
check: Marbury v. Madison was decided in...
The Court can strike down ___ laws.
lessons.try: Explain the significance of Marbury v. Madison.

learn: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ended legal school segregation.
Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) guaranteed lawyers for poor defendants.
Miranda v. Arizona (1966) requires police to inform suspects of their rights.
lessons.try: Present a landmark case: facts, question, decision and impact.

units.t: Federalism and State and Local Government

learn: Federalism divides power between national and state governments.
Delegated powers belong to the nation; reserved powers to the states (10th Amendment); concurrent powers are shared.
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme.
check: Running schools is mainly a ___ power.
The Supremacy Clause makes ___ law supreme.
lessons.try: Sort powers into delegated, reserved and concurrent.

learn: States have constitutions, governors, legislatures and courts.
States handle education, policing, licences and elections.
Many states allow ballot initiatives and referendums.
check: A state's chief executive is the...
lessons.try: Research your state's governor and legislature.

learn: Counties, cities and towns provide police, fire, water, roads and parks.
Mayors and councils lead cities; school boards run districts.
Local government is closest to citizens.
check: Cities are often led by a...
lessons.try: Attend or watch a city council or school board meeting.

units.t: Civil Liberties: The Bill of Rights

learn: Protects freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly and petition.
Rights have limits: true threats and defamation are not protected.
Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected student speech that doesn't disrupt school.
check: The First Amendment protects freedom of...
lessons.try: Analyse a student speech scenario using Tinker.

learn: The 4th Amendment bars unreasonable searches; warrants need probable cause.
The 5th protects against self-incrimination and double jeopardy; the 6th guarantees a speedy, public trial and a lawyer.
The 8th bans cruel and unusual punishment and excessive bail.
check: Double jeopardy is protected by the ___ Amendment.
lessons.try: Role-play a scenario applying the 4th Amendment.

learn: The 2nd Amendment addresses the right to bear arms.
The 9th says listed rights don't deny others; the 10th reserves powers.
The 14th Amendment applies most of the Bill of Rights to states (incorporation).
check: The 9th Amendment says listed rights don't ___ others.
lessons.try: Explain incorporation with one example.

learn: The 13th (1865) abolished slavery; the 14th (1868) gave citizenship and equal protection; the 15th (1870) banned racial discrimination in voting.
Jim Crow laws and Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) undermined these rights.
Brown v. Board overturned "separate but equal" in schools.
check: Slavery was abolished by the ___ Amendment.
Equal protection is in the ___ Amendment.
lessons.try: Trace equal protection from Plessy to Brown.

learn: The Civil Rights Act (1964) banned discrimination in public places and jobs.
The Voting Rights Act (1965) protected Black voters.
Nonviolent protest (Montgomery, Selma, March on Washington) drove change.
check: The Voting Rights Act was passed in...
The Civil Rights Act banned discrimination in...
lessons.try: Analyse how a protest led to a law.

learn: The 19th Amendment (1920) gave women the vote.
The Americans with Disabilities Act (1990) protects people with disabilities.
Courts and legislatures continue to define equal protection.
lessons.try: Research a current civil rights issue and the arguments on different sides.

learn: Parties nominate candidates, organise campaigns and shape policy.
Primaries choose party nominees; general elections choose officials.
The Electoral College elects the president; 270 of 538 votes are needed.
lessons.try: Map how the Electoral College works.

learn: Citizens 18 and older may vote (26th Amendment, 1971); registration rules vary by state.
Evaluate media for bias, sourcing and fact-checking.
Interest groups and PACs try to influence policy.
check: The voting age became 18 with the ___ Amendment.
lessons.try: Fact-check a political claim using two reliable sources.

learn: Citizens participate by voting, volunteering, contacting officials, serving on juries and peaceful protest.
Civil discourse means disagreeing respectfully.
Young people can lead change in their communities.
check: Contacting officials is a form of...
lessons.try: Plan a civic action project on a local issue.
